# The throw Keyword

#### Course: Learn C++ Intermediate

## The throw Keyword

This is the try...catch statement we used in our previous program.

```cpp
try {
      
    cout << "Enter denominator: ";
    cin >> denominator;

    // throw an exception if denominator is 0
    if (denominator == 0)
        throw 0;

    double result = numerator / denominator;

    cout << "Result: " << result;
}

catch (int num) {
    cout << "Denominator cannot be 0. Try again.";
}
```

Notice the throw 0; statement in our program. The throw statement is used to manually trigger an exception so that it can be "caught" by the catch block.

We've already discussed why it's a good practice to manually throw an exception when it comes to floating-point exceptions. If you've forgotten why, then you should revisit the previous lesson: C++ Exceptions.

Back to our program, notice that we've "thrown" the integer 0 when we encounter the exception. This value is "caught" by the num parameter in the catch block.

```cpp
catch (int num) {
    cout << "Denominator cannot be 0. Try again.";
}
```

Thus, the data type of the thrown value and the data type of the catch parameter must be the same.

We can also use the num parameter in our error message. For example, we can replace the catch block above with the one below.

```cpp
catch (int num) {
    cout << "Denominator cannot be " << num << ". Try again.";
}
```

Both these catch blocks give the same output.

![When an exception occurs, the throw statement directs the program flow to the catch block. Otherwise, the remaining statements inside the try block are executed.](data:image/png;base64,)
